messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 32
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Housekeeper
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 61

He is 32, a South Asian man who has been married for six years, and he works as a housekeeper in a downtown hotel. Before the robbery, his life is quiet and structured. He wakes before dawn, makes tea for himself and his wife, and takes the bus across the city in his housekeeping uniform, the spare one folded carefully in his backpack in case he needs to change after a shift. He likes the predictability of his work: the cart lined up with fresh towels, the smell of detergent, the satisfaction of leaving a room orderly and clean. He is not someone who seeks attention. He takes pride in being reliable, in sending money to his parents when he can, in building a stable life.

The robbery happens on an evening in late autumn. He has just finished a shift that runs later than usual because a guest on one floor leaves several rooms in disarray. He misses his usual bus and decides to walk a few blocks to a different stop. The street is dim, not empty but quiet enough that he notices footsteps before he sees the men. Two of them approach quickly. At first he thinks they are asking for directions. Then one grabs his jacket and shoves him hard against a wall. The other demands his wallet and phone. He remembers the smell of cigarettes on one man’s breath, the scrape of brick against the back of his head, and the strange clarity with which he sees his own hotel ID badge swinging from his neck. He hands over what he has, but one of the men hits him anyway. He is certain, in that instant, that they may kill him. He does not fight back. He hears his own voice begging, though later he hates himself for remembering that. When they run, he slides down the wall and sits on the pavement for several minutes, dizzy, ashamed, and unable to stand.

In the first days afterward, he tells almost no one the full story. He says he was “robbed” in a flat, practical tone, as if naming it will contain it. His wife sees the bruising along his cheek and shoulder and urges him to go to the police, which he does, but he speaks haltingly and feels foolish when he cannot remember details in order. At home he starts checking the door lock repeatedly, returning from the bedroom to the front door three or four times each night. When his wife reaches for him unexpectedly, he flinches so sharply that both of them freeze. Sleep becomes fractured. He wakes soaked in sweat after dreams in which he is pinned and voiceless, or in which he is walking a hotel corridor and the men step out of a guest room as if they belong there.

As the weeks pass, the fear spreads into ordinary parts of his day. On the bus he scans every face that gets on. If two young men laugh behind him, his chest tightens and his hands grow cold. He begins getting off one stop early or late to avoid the corner where the robbery happened, even if it means a longer walk in daylight. If he has to work the evening shift, he feels sick from the moment he wakes. At the hotel, he tells himself he is safe, but his body does not believe it. The slam of a heavy door on a hallway can make him jerk so violently he drops folded linens. When guests approach from behind to ask for extra towels, he spins around before they finish speaking, heart pounding, embarrassed by the alarm on their faces.

He had once been known at work as quiet but warm, someone who exchanged easy greetings with the front desk staff and joked gently with the laundry attendants. Now he keeps his head down. He avoids the staff entrance after dark and waits for coworkers to leave in groups so he does not have to walk alone to the bus. If no one is available, he sometimes pays for a ride home they cannot really afford. He tells his wife they need to be careful with money, but then spends extra on small things that make him feel prepared: a brighter flashlight, another lock, a portable alarm. She notices that he no longer wants to visit friends in the evening or stop at the grocery store after work. Their world narrows to work and home.

What disturbs him most is not only the fear but the change in how he sees himself. He was raised to believe a man should be able to protect himself and his family. Since the mugging, he carries a persistent shame that feels heavier than the bruise ever did. He replays the moment against the wall and thinks, I did nothing. He knows, rationally, that handing over his wallet likely kept him alive, but the thought does not settle the feeling. He grows irritable over small things—an unwashed cup in the sink, a delayed bus, his wife asking when he will be home. Then he feels guilty immediately afterward. Some nights he sits awake in the dark living room rather than coming to bed, listening for sounds in the hallway of their apartment building.

Months later, he is still organized and dutiful at work, still making beds with tight corners and replacing toiletries with care, but every shift takes effort that no one sees. He moves through the city as if danger is just outside the frame of each moment. He wants his old life back—the ordinary tiredness after work, the casual walk to the bus stop, the ability to hear footsteps behind him without feeling his body prepare for another blow. Instead, he lives with a constant sense that the world has already shown him what can happen, and could do so again at any time.
